name: Jacobin
summary: Jacobinism is the revolutionary republicanism of the Jacobin Club and its Montagnard leaders, above all Robespierre. It held that sovereignty lies in the people and is indivisible, that a centralised republic should be defended by civic virtue and, in crisis, by terror, and that property and wealth should serve the public good without abolishing private ownership.
scope: The Montagnard Jacobins of 1793-94 around Robespierre and Saint-Just, based on Robespierre's 1793 declaration of rights and 1794 report on political morality, the Constitution of 1793 and reference accounts. Excludes the pre-1792 constitutional monarchist club, Girondins, and later uses of 'Jacobin' for any centralist.

universal-healthcare.rationale: The 1793 Constitution added a right to public assistance, which supports state-guaranteed care for those in need.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Generally pro-market in principle, but the Jacobins imposed general price maxima and requisitions when markets failed in wartime.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Robespierre proposed exempting those below subsistence and progressive taxation by size of fortune.

property-fundamental.rationale: The 1793 Constitution guaranteed property, yet Robespierre limited it by the duty to respect others' rights and the right to existence.

cut-welfare.rationale: The 1793 Constitution recognised public assistance as a social debt.

worker-ownership.rationale: Robespierre called community of goods a chimera; wide property for individuals, not collective ownership.

surveillance-ok.rationale: The Law of Suspects authorised detention on vague suspicion in defence of the Republic.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Speech against the Republic was prosecuted as counterrevolutionary, though hate speech as such was not the issue.

strong-leader.rationale: Rule was by committees of the Convention, and Robespierre cast his rule as virtue serving the people, not a personal leader bypassing it.

state-harmful.rationale: Jacobinism centres on a sovereign, indivisible public authority over civil society.

decide-locally.rationale: Jacobins built a strong centralised government and defended indivisible sovereignty.

rehabilitation.rationale: Terror was justice that is prompt, severe and inflexible.

more-religion-public.rationale: Jacobins rejected both the Church and atheism and created civic cults, so split.

gradual-change.rationale: Jacobins were revolutionary and overturned existing institutions.

reduce-immigration.rationale: The 1793 Constitution offered refuge to those from tyrannised nations.

free-trade.rationale: Generally favoured free trade in principle but imposed price maxima in crisis.

nation-first.rationale: Robespierre proclaimed brotherhood of all peoples, yet the Republic's defence came first.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: The 1793 Constitution barred interference in other governments.

revolution-justified.rationale: The Jacobins made the revolution and the 1793 Constitution declared a duty to rebel against oppression.

experts-over-public.rationale: Popular sovereignty was the core principle.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Requisitioning for war, but no investment policy.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Extreme inequality of wealth was condemned while community of goods was called a chimera.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Robespierre rejected community of goods as a chimera.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: The republic dealt with citizens, not state bodies of employers and workers; wage maxima were set by the state.

one-party-rule.rationale: Montagnard-led government suppressed rival factions, but there was no single-party state.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: The club became republican and the monarchy was abolished.

democracy-best.rationale: Terror was called a natural consequence of democracy; virtue was the spring of popular government.

direct-votes.rationale: The 1793 Constitution had popular ratification and a communal veto on bills.

right-to-secede.rationale: Indivisible sovereignty; the Vendee revolt was crushed.

natural-rulers.rationale: Robespierre denounced aristocrats and kings as rebels against humanity.

political-violence-never.rationale: Robespierre's 1794 speech calls terror an emanation of virtue and a consequence of democracy, saying that in a revolution virtue without terror is powerless.

war-builds-character.rationale: Robespierre opposed the 1792 war with Austria.

separate-church-state.rationale: Pushed for separation of church and state but created state civic cults.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: They rejected the Church and replaced it with civic cults.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Revolutionary Tribunal and national army as state functions.

ethnic-nation.rationale: A civic nation of citizens; all people are brothers.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Robespierre appealed to citizens and the people against tyrants, not to class war.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Equality of goods was called a chimera.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Virtue as devotion to the public good is the spring of the republic.

duties-before-rights.rationale: Virtue meant subordinating private interest to the fatherland.

restore-past-order.rationale: Robespierre's 1794 speech aims to replace the vices of the monarchy with the virtues of a republic, and calls a slide back into aristocracy or monarchy the death of the body politic.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Policy was driven by principles of virtue and equality.

direct-action.rationale: Worked through the Convention but also relied on popular insurrection.

means-match-ends.rationale: Revolutionary government as despotism of liberty against tyranny.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Subsistence guaranteed but community of goods rejected.

production-for-use.rationale: Commerce was to serve public wealth, but profit was not abolished.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Revolutionary dictatorship was by the Convention for the people, not one class.

taxation-theft.rationale: Robespierre proposed that citizens with only subsistence incomes be exempt and that others bear public expenses progressively according to their wealth, treating taxation as a civic duty.

conscription.rationale: The levee en masse of August 1793 mobilised the nation.

state-as-business.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-12): its value turns on whether citizens are customers who can leave, and the statement now asks only whether government should be run on business principles.

reviewHistory.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-12): its value turns on whether citizens are customers who can leave, and the statement now asks only whether government should be run on business principles.

positive-liberty.rationale: Robespierre tied property and liberty to subsistence for all.

organic-representation.rationale: Individual citizens and national sovereignty, not corporate bodies.

total-state.rationale: The Constitution protected religion and rights, even though the Terror was extensive.

national-rebirth.rationale: Regeneration of the nation through virtue.

territorial-expansion.rationale: The Constitution called France friend and ally of free nations.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Robespierre's proposed declaration calls kings, aristocrats and tyrants slaves in rebellion against the sovereign of the earth, the human race.

bound-labor.rationale: The Convention's decree of 17 July 1793 abolished all remaining seigneurial dues without compensation, ending legal obligations of peasants to lords.

universal-morality.rationale: Robespierre invoked the Legislator of Nature and universal rights.

school-vouchers.rationale: Widespread public education was a Jacobin aim.

rule-by-example.rationale: Lead the people by reason and enemies by terror.

national-self-determination.rationale: Brotherhood of peoples and opposition to oppressing nations.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Cult of Reason yet Robespierre opposed atheism.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Robespierre held the republic served the people.

national-mission.rationale: Robespierre opposed armed missionaries; yet republic as model.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its rationale is about one government, party or regime, or about fighting corruption, not a general claim that most politicians put their own interests first, which this statement now asks.

reviewHistory.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its rationale is about one government, party or regime, or about fighting corruption, not a general claim that most politicians put their own interests first, which this statement now asks.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: Terror itself was state violence defended as justice.

night-watchman-state.rationale: State guarantees subsistence and public education.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Men of all lands are brothers.

restrict-conversion.rationale: 1793 Constitution guaranteed free exercise of religion.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: Revolutionary government as despotism of liberty during war against enemies.

consent-of-governed.rationale: The 1793 Constitution asserted popular sovereignty and added a right, and duty, of insurrection when the government violates the rights of the people.

separated-powers.rationale: Committees concentrated power in the Convention.

vanguard-party.rationale: Lenin adopted Jacobin centralised revolutionary organisation.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Robespierre criticised the declaration as written for the rich.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: Inequality blamed on institutions rather than population, as in Robespierre's speech.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Revolutionary force and terror were defended as justice against enemies of liberty.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: The Law of Suspects and Revolutionary Tribunal set aside ordinary protections, and Robespierre defended terror as prompt, severe justice.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: The Law of the General Maximum fixed grain and staple prices and was enforced by revolutionary armies.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: The Jacobin Club enforced a unified line through purges of members, and Robespierre required unity behind the Committee of Public Safety.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Jacobins held sovereignty to be indivisible and rested in the people of the single French republic, so a binding supranational body contradicts it.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Jacobins ruled through the Convention and its committees, and opposed monarchic executive power, with the 1793 Constitution placing the executive under the legislature.

church-by-bishops.rationale: The Jacobin line favored the Civil Constitution of the Clergy with elected clergy and later de-Christianization and the Cult of the Supreme Being, against episcopal authority.

clerical-rule.rationale: Jacobins were anticlerical republicans who placed sovereignty in the people and replaced church authority with civic cults.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Jacobins ran the revolutionary war effort, with the levee en masse and the defense of the nation as their first duty.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Robespierre made civic virtue the foundation of the republic, and the Jacobins used festivals, theatre control and censorship to shape republican morals.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: Robespierre limited property and favored a wide distribution of it, but did not abolish rent or private ownership.

people-in-arms.rationale: The levee en masse and the 1793 constitution's right of insurrection and civic armed duty favored a citizen-army.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: Jacobins stressed a single indivisible republic of France, but they did not address divided nations as such.

death-penalty.rationale: The Terror used execution on a vast scale against enemies of the republic, and Robespierre defended it as justice.

creationism-in-schools.rationale: The Jacobins promoted a civic cult of the Supreme Being and Enlightenment reason, and rejected church doctrine in education.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: The French republic treated citizens as made by the political community and grew citizenship by law, not by descent alone.

minority-language-support.rationale: The indivisible republic imposed French on the regions, and the Convention in 1794 decreed French as the sole language.

religious-exemptions.rationale: Robespierre and the Jacobins demanded a unified law for all citizens and policed religion as a threat to republican unity.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Jacobin civic virtue demanded conformity to republican values; eccentricity was suspect in the Terror.

constituent-assembly.rationale: The Convention was elected to draft a new republican constitution, and the 1793 Constitution was then put to a popular vote.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: Revolutionary government suspended ordinary liberties for the Terror, and Robespierre defended it as necessary to secure the Republic.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Robespierre's 1793 declaration limits property by the duty not to harm the rights of others and by the needs of society.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: The Jacobins subordinated the clergy to the state and attacked church property, while Robespierre kept a civic religion.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: The Jacobins crushed the Federalist revolts and the Vendee to preserve the one and indivisible Republic.

region-keeps-system.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-12): its rationale rests on general self-government, separate laws or no stated position, not on keeping a distinct economic system, and the statement now asks only whether a region joining a larger state should be free to keep its economic system.

reviewHistory.rationale: Jacobinism is defined by centralisation and indivisible sovereignty, leaving no room for regional autonomy.

sacred-ruler.rationale: The Jacobins abolished the monarchy and executed the king.

flat-income-tax.rationale: Robespierre's declaration called for progressive taxation, the opposite of a flat tax.

character-from-environment.rationale: Robespierre's emphasis on public education and civic virtue rests on the view that institutions shape citizens.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Law was the expression of the general will and rulers were bound by it, though revolutionary government suspended the constitution.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Indivisible popular sovereignty in a single assembly rejects blending powers between few and many.

leader-cult.rationale: Robespierre denounced individual idolatry, though the Jacobins did honor martyrs and a civic cult.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: Jacobinism meant an indivisible, centralised republic with no separate self-governing national institutions.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: The general will, the 1793 referendum and popular sovereignty put majority will above other institutions.

gender-parity-bodies.rationale: The Jacobin Club and the republic excluded women from political life.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Wartime controls and the levee en masse had autarkic features, but no stated policy of a closed bloc.

moral-incentives.rationale: Robespierre made civic virtue and a sense of public duty the principle of the republic.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: The Revolution abolished hereditary nobility and the Jacobins stood for equality of citizens.

patriotic-education.rationale: Jacobins promoted civic education, national festivals and the civic cults to instill republican virtue and patriotism.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: The Jacobins issued a declaration of rights and the 1793 Constitution, though rights could be suspended under revolutionary government.

elective-rulers.rationale: Sovereignty belongs to the people and magistrates are elected; hereditary kingship was abolished.

minority-veto.rationale: Sovereignty and the general will are indivisible; no minority or member may block the people's decision.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: The 1793 declaration and constitution make insurrection the people's right and duty when government violates their rights.

parliament-supreme.rationale: The Convention held sovereign legislative power as the people's representatives, though in practice the Committee of Public Safety dominated.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Jacobins rejected aristocratic privilege and treated assistance to the poor as a right owed by society, not charity from the privileged.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Robespierre demanded active civic virtue from all citizens in service of the republic.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: Robespierre's declaration proclaims rights as universal to all peoples, not dependent on civilization.

military-guardian-role.rationale: Armies were subordinated to the Convention through representatives on mission; a political role for generals was feared.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Robespierre's republic of virtue opposed luxury and corrupting wealth.

job-guarantee.rationale: The 1793 Constitution declared public assistance a sacred debt, covering work for the able-bodied poor.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Jacobins demanded obedience to the general will and the law, while keeping a right to insurrection against tyranny.

non-intervention.rationale: The 1793 Constitution renounced interfering in other nations' governments, yet the Jacobins fought a revolutionary war to spread liberty; the record is split.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: The Jacobins saw conspiracies by aristocrats, priests and foreign powers, but these were political rather than ethnic or religious minorities as such.

informal-organisation.rationale: The Jacobins were a disciplined national network of affiliated clubs and distrusted factions.

national-law-over-international.rationale: Indivisible national sovereignty was central, and the people's law was held to override any outside authority.

religious-nation.rationale: Robespierre's Cult of the Supreme Being was civic rather than confessional, and the republic defined citizenship by civic virtue, not a shared church.

regional-revenue-retention.rationale: Jacobins held the republic one and indivisible and treated federalism as a Girondin threat, so regions would not keep their own revenue.

personal-possessions-private.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-12): its value rests on accepting or rejecting common ownership of production, or on private property in general, and the statement now asks only whether personal belongings should stay private where production is held in common.

reviewHistory.rationale: Robespierre limited property and taxed wealth progressively but defended private ownership, so he would not extend common ownership to production.

religion-illusion.rationale: Robespierre denounced atheism and promoted a civic cult of the Supreme Being, treating religion as socially useful, not an illusion.

treaties-binding.rationale: With sovereignty one and indivisible, there are no internal nations with treaty standing; the state may change its own laws.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: The 1791 revolutionary penal code dropped sodomy as an offence, but Jacobin moralism and the Year II republic of virtue were hostile to it, so adherents were not strongly against criminalisation.

suppress-opposition.rationale: The Law of Suspects and the Terror suppressed opponents and clubs to defend the republic, and Robespierre justified terror as virtue's emanation.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: The Jacobins pursued dechristianisation and a civic cult of the Supreme Being while the Constitution of 1793 guaranteed worship; punishing blasphemy in favour of a religion was not their aim.

defensive-jihad-duty.rationale: The Jacobins did not address Islamic doctrine; their own analogue was the levee en masse for national defence, but this statement is out of scope.

participatory-democracy.rationale: The Jacobins backed popular sections, political clubs, and the Constitution of 1793's referendum and universal male suffrage, though revolutionary government centralised decisions.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Robespierre's declaration placed sovereignty in the people, and the Jacobins rejected the divine right of kings.

social-market-economy.rationale: Jacobins accepted private property and a market with price maxima and relief, resembling neither laissez-faire nor a modern social market; the match is loose.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: The Jacobins organised the levee en masse and a citizen army to defend the republic.

rich-first.rationale: Robespierre's declaration limited property by its social usefulness and favoured progressive taxation, rejecting letting some grow rich while others wait.

dynastic-succession.rationale: The Jacobins overthrew the monarchy and rejected hereditary privilege; popular sovereignty excludes inherited office.

property-franchise.rationale: Robespierre condemned the property-based franchise and the Constitution of 1793 established universal male suffrage.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: The revolutionary government of 1793-94 ruled by emergency decrees and the Law of Suspects, setting aside ordinary standing-law constraints.

racial-franchise.rationale: The Jacobin conception of equal citizenship and the 1793 constitution rejected restricting political rights to a group; abolition of slavery in 1794 followed this.

interfaith-marriage-restriction.rationale: The Revolution secularised marriage as a civil contract; Jacobin republicanism opposed religious legal distinctions.

reinterpret-religion.rationale: Robespierre rejected Church authority and promoted a rationalist Cult of the Supreme Being; applying this to religious doctrine is an inference.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Robespierre's 1793 declaration made property subordinate to the public good and condemned extreme inequality of fortune as a threat to republican liberty.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: Robespierre opposed the dechristianisation campaign and instead set up the Cult of the Supreme Being, so the state promoted a civic deism, not atheism.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: The Jacobin republic relied on policing, revolutionary tribunals and imprisonment of suspects as core instruments of the Terror.

power-sharing-divided-societies.rationale: Sovereignty was held to be one and indivisible, which excludes guaranteed shares of power for particular communities.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: The 1793 Constitution made public assistance a sacred debt of society, placing relief of the poor on the state rather than on charity.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: Robespierre held that property must serve the public good and that society owes subsistence to citizens, rather than rewarding mere wealth.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: The Jacobins defended the republic by terror and Robespierre made virtue and terror joint principles, so killing for the public good was justified.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: Robespierre's report presents politics as a moral contest between virtue and vice and he later established the Cult of the Supreme Being.

single-unit-for-people.rationale: The Jacobins imposed uniform departments and opposed regional particularism and federalism in the name of an indivisible republic.

second-chamber.rationale: The Constitution of 1793 vested legislative power in a single unicameral assembly, as the sovereign people's delegate.

municipal-property.rationale: Robespierre limited property and taxed wealth progressively but kept private ownership; no municipal ownership was proposed.

confederal-coordination.rationale: Jacobins were centralisers who attacked the Girondins as federalists and defended an indivisible republic.

person-over-state.rationale: Robespierre held that virtue and terror served the republic and its people, so individuals could be sacrificed to the public good.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Robespierre promoted the civic Cult of the Supreme Being and the immortality of the soul as moral foundations of the republic.

regional-powers-revocable.rationale: The republic was one and indivisible and departments were agents of the Convention, which could override them.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: Contested: the 1793 Constitution rejects conquest, yet the Jacobin republic waged revolutionary war and levée en masse.

communal-electorates.rationale: Indivisible sovereignty and a single body of citizens rule out separate religious electorates.

foreign-partition-plot.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-12): its rationale rests on whether a foreign plot is believed to exist, or on foreign hostility in general rather than territorial partition, and the statement now asks whether preventing foreign-backed partition should be a central aim of national policy.

reviewHistory.rationale: Robespierre denounced foreign conspiracies and a foreign faction aiming to destroy the Republic, and the Terror targeted them.

soldiers-refuse-war.rationale: The republic fought a war of national defence and treated desertion and refusal of duty as treason against the patrie.

sacred-nation.rationale: Robespierre made love of the patrie and the indivisible people central to republican virtue, and the Cult of the Supreme Being gave the republic a quasi-sacred character.

shared-human-nature.rationale: The 1793 declaration grounds universal natural rights in human nature, though the Jacobins also sought to regenerate citizens through virtue.

one-language-many-names.rationale: Jacobins pushed French as the single national language yet treated regional speech as patois; no clear stance on naming.

customary-chiefs-lawmaking.rationale: Indivisible popular sovereignty left no place for hereditary or customary authorities in lawmaking.

mandatory-sentences.rationale: The Law of 22 Prairial made death the fixed penalty for convicted enemies, showing preference for rigid severity.

democracy-is-procedure.rationale: Robespierre held that government in crisis rests on virtue and terror, not only on elections.

women-suffrage.rationale: The 1793 Constitution gave the vote to men only, and the Jacobin-led Convention closed women's political clubs in 1793.

homestead-ownership.rationale: Robespierre's 1793 declaration defines property by law and limits it by its duty to society, rejecting an absolute first-claim right.

scripture-inerrant.rationale: Jacobins favoured a deist civic cult of the Supreme Being and dechristianisation pressures over revealed, literal religion.

national-church-status.rationale: The Jacobins opposed a privileged church and promoted a state civic religion instead of the traditional national church.

minority-territorial-autonomy.rationale: The republic was one and indivisible and the Jacobins crushed federalism, so territorial autonomy was rejected.

simple-living.rationale: Robespierre made civic virtue, frugality and austerity the basis of the republic.

equal-conscription.rationale: The levee en masse called up men, and women were excluded from arms and political clubs.

extrajudicial-killing.rationale: Not about drugs; the Terror used revolutionary tribunals and the Law of Suspects rather than killing without any process, though the line was thin.

bypass-parties-groups.rationale: Jacobins denounced factions yet organised through their own club and committees; adherents' view is mixed.

no-business-privileges.rationale: Jacobins attacked speculators and hoarders and imposed the maximum, opposing monopolistic privilege.

no-denominational-politics.rationale: The Jacobin Club was republican and secular, promoting a civic cult of the Supreme Being above confessional division.

distribution-by-process.rationale: Robespierre held that property is limited by the duty to society and that extreme inequality is incompatible with republican liberty, so process alone does not justify a fortune.

patriotism-serves-workers.rationale: Jacobin patriotism was bound to the sans-culottes and the people, and the levee en masse defended the republic of ordinary citizens.

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: The 1793 Constitution recognised public assistance as a social debt. (Carried over from cut-welfare, "Welfare programs create dependency and should be cut.", with the value reversed, 2026-11-11.)

missingStatements.text: In a national emergency, a government may suspend ordinary legal protections to defeat its internal enemies.
missingStatements.rationale: The Law of Suspects and Revolutionary Tribunal suspended ordinary protections, and Robespierre defended terror as prompt, severe justice.

missingStatements.text: Governments should fix maximum prices for essential foods in times of scarcity.
missingStatements.rationale: The Law of the General Maximum fixed grain and staple prices, enforced by revolutionary armies.

notes: Jacobins were pragmatic on economics: generally pro-market in principle but driven to controls by war. Many answers are low-confidence inferences.
